papers.title: Surface code logical operations on a superconducting quantum processor
papers.abstract: Fault-tolerant quantum computation requires logical operations that manipulate encoded information while preserving quantum error-correction protection. In planar surface-code architectures, code deformation and lattice surgery provide a local, measurement-based route to such operations. Here we experimentally realize key elements of patch-based surface-code logical processing on a 107-qubit superconducting quantum processor. We first implement a reusable primitive layer comprising merge and split, patch expansion and shrinkage, and deformations mediated by domain walls and twist defects. We then compose these primitives to realize logical state routing, the logical controlled-NOT gate, and the single-qubit Hadamard and phase gates, which together form a Clifford-generating set. All operations are implemented on distance-three rotated surface-code patches with multi-round syndrome extraction and neural-network decoding, without post-selection. Our results advance superconducting surface-code experiments from protected logical memory to active, patch-based fault-tolerant logical operations.

summary.summary: This work demonstrates key elements of patch-based surface-code logical processing on a 107-qubit superconducting processor, implementing code-deformation and lattice-surgery primitives (merge, split, expansion, shrinkage, domain walls, twist defects) and composing them into a Clifford-generating set of logical gates (H, S, CNOT) on distance-3 rotated surface-code patches with multi-round syndrome extraction and neural-network decoding. All operations are performed without post-selection, advancing superconducting surface-code experiments from protected logical memory to active, measurement-based logical operations.
summary.motivation: Fault-tolerant quantum computation requires logical operations that manipulate encoded information while maintaining error-correction protection, but the locality constraints of surface codes restrict transversal gate implementations. Code deformation and lattice surgery provide a measurement-based route to such operations through reconfigurable patch geometries and boundaries.
summary.method: On the Zuchongzhi 3.2 processor with average 1Q error $1.01 \times 10^{-3}$, CZ error $5.06 \times 10^{-3}$, and readout error $1.11 \times 10^{-2}$, the authors implemented logical state routing via lattice-surgery teleportation and code deformation, logical CNOT via ancilla-mediated parity measurements using a $7 \times 7$ footprint and 6 QEC cycles, logical H via geometric patch rotation combined with a Hadamard domain wall using a $3 \times 5$ footprint and 6 cycles, and logical S via gate teleportation with fault-tolerant $|+i\rangle$ ancilla using a $3 \times 7$ footprint and 4–5 cycles. All circuits use distance-3 patches and neural-network decoding of the syndrome record.
summary.result: Decoded logical state fidelities for routing: $0.908$–$0.911$ for Z-basis states, $0.841$–$0.863$ for X-basis states. Logical CNOT Bell-state fidelities: $0.550$–$0.624$, all above the separability bound of $0.5$; average PTM fidelity $0.643(2)$. Logical H gate: PTM elements $R_{X \to Z} = 0.796(2)$, $R_{Z \to X} = 0.784(5)$, $R_{Y \to Y} = -0.546(4)$; average gate fidelity $0.854(1)$. Logical S gate: PTM elements $R_{X \to Y} = 0.589(3)$, $R_{Y \to -X} = -0.587(3)$, $R_{Z \to Z} = 0.901(3)$; average gate fidelity $0.846(1)$. Circuit-level distance verification confirms all distance-3 gates are distance-preserving; simulations indicate logical-error suppression with distance enters a pronounced regime when physical error rates are reduced to $\approx 50\%$ of present values.

papers.title: High-Precision Calibration Workflow Achieves Above $99.9\%$ CZ Gate Fidelity on a Scalable Superconducting Processor
papers.abstract: High-fidelity universal two-qubit gates are critical for building fault-tolerant quantum computers. In scalable superconducting processors, shortened coherence times introduce more incoherent errors in gate operations. With a constrained error budget, there is reduced tolerance for coherent errors stemming from parameter deviations. In this work, we develop a closed-loop workflow to enhance the CZ gate calibration precision. Utilizing the echoed leakage error amplification (ELEA) and the repurposed context-aware fidelity estimation (CAFE) circuits, we suppress the population leakage to non-computational states, and, for the first time, demonstrate a CZ gate fidelity exceeding $99.9\%$ on an 84-qubit processor, with coherent error suppressed to $0.007\%$. Meanwhile, we obtain a median fidelity of $99.25\%$ among 72 CZ gates, demonstrating that the workflow can be generalized to the calibration of parallel CZ gates. Finally, we realize automated calibration and observe enhanced stability of the CZ gate throughout 9-hour comparative monitoring experiments. Our results, realized on a completely domestic platform, establish an efficient and automated route to quantum computation with superconducting quantum systems.

similar_to.title: Above 99.9% Fidelity Single-Qubit Gates, Two-Qubit Gates, and Readout in a Single Superconducting Quantum Device
Logic gates at the surface code threshold: Superconducting qubits poised for fault-tolerant quantum computing

summary.summary: This work develops a closed-loop calibration workflow combining echoed leakage error amplification (ELEA) and context-aware fidelity estimation (CAFE) circuits to achieve CZ gate fidelity exceeding $99.9\%$ on an 84-qubit superconducting processor with tunable transmon qubits and couplers. Automated recalibration every 0.5 hours maintains gate stability over 9-hour monitoring periods, with median fidelity $99.25\%$ across 72 parallel CZ gates and coherent error suppressed to $0.007\%$.
summary.motivation: Scalable superconducting processors suffer from increased incoherent errors due to TLS defects and crosstalk from high control-line density, leaving reduced tolerance for coherent calibration errors. Achieving CZ fidelities near the $0.1\%$ error threshold for fault-tolerant quantum error correction on multi-qubit processors requires precise parameter tuning and automated stabilization.
summary.method: A three-stage calibration workflow iteratively applies SEA (for Z-interaction tuning), ELEA (for leakage suppression to state $|02\rangle$), and CAFE (fine amplitude and phase calibration) circuits. Flux pulse amplitudes $A_1, A_2, A_c$ are optimized using hyperbolic pulse shaping with $\eta=10$, $T=48$ ns gate duration, and virtual $Z$ phases compensate single-qubit errors. Automated recalibration repeats the fine CAFE stage every 0.5 hours to track environmental drift.
summary.result: Maximum single-pair CZ fidelity reached $(99.92 \pm 0.01)\%$ with incoherent error $0.079\%$ and coherent error $0.007\%$, and leakage error $< 0.001\%$; median fidelity across 72 gates was $(99.25 \pm 0.01)\%$ with median error rate $0.75\%$. Automated calibration reduced error rate drift significantly in high-fluctuation qubits (e.g., Q$69$, Q$62$) over 9-hour periods compared to calibration-free control, with median single-qubit error $0.05\%$ (randomized benchmarking, $14$ ns pulses with DRAG).

papers.title: Bit flips are erasures in dissipative cat qubits
papers.abstract: Autonomous quantum error correction (QEC) stabilizes a logical manifold through dissipative events that emit into output channels, which are typically accessible to measurement. These signals are often discarded, and whether they contain useful information about logical failures remains generally unclear. Using quantum trajectories, we show that in dissipatively stabilized cat qubits bit flips are not silent logical errors: each flip is accompanied by a strong, time-localized photon burst from the dissipative buffer. Photon counting and homodyne monitoring can therefore herald the loss of logical information without interrupting the autonomous stabilization: bit flips in dissipative cat qubits are erasures. More broadly, our results show that the emitted signals of engineered reservoirs can act as built-in failure monitors for autonomous QEC, turning rare logical faults into erasures available to a decoder and reducing fault-tolerance overhead. To this end, we develop a general framework, based on past quantum states and number-resolved master equations, to quantify the detectability of such logical failures in autonomous QEC from the emitted signal.

similar_to.title: Quantum control of a cat-qubit with bit-flip times exceeding ten seconds
Exponential suppression of bit-flips in a qubit encoded in an oscillator

summary.summary: This paper shows that bit-flip errors in dissipatively stabilized cat qubits are detectable erasures, heralded by strong, time-localized photon bursts from the dissipative buffer used for autonomous quantum error correction. The authors develop a framework based on past quantum states and number-resolved master equations to quantify the detectability of logical failures from emitted signals in autonomous QEC, demonstrating viability with realistic photodetector parameters.
summary.motivation: Autonomous QEC dissipates errors into output channels that are typically discarded, leaving unclear whether they contain useful information about logical failures. Understanding whether emitted signals can herald logical errors without interrupting stabilization would reduce fault-tolerance overhead.
summary.method: Using quantum trajectories, past quantum state formalism, and number-resolved master equations, the authors analyze the buffer emission conditioned on bit-flip events in cat qubits with parameters $g/2\pi = 5$ MHz, $\kappa_a/2\pi = \kappa_\phi/2\pi = 10$ kHz, $\kappa_b/2\pi = 100$ MHz. They establish a threshold criterion for photon counting and investigate robustness to detector imperfections ($\eta = 70\%$, dark count rate $\gamma_d/2\pi = 1$ kHz).
summary.result: Bit flips generate $\mathcal{E}$ photons from the buffer that grows with cat size $\langle a^\dagger a \rangle$, with strong separation between flip and no-flip distributions. At realistic parameters, photon counting achieves high distinguishability $P(n|\mathrm{BF})$ and $P(n|\neg\mathrm{BF})$ with minimal overlap, enabling threshold-based erasure detection that improves with cat size; homodyne detection remains viable with Cauchy-Schwarz coherence $\mathcal{C} \gtrsim 0.9$ for $\langle a^\dagger a \rangle \geq 2$.

papers.title: Idling error suppression through gate scheduling
papers.abstract: Achieving high-precision quantum computation requires effective suppression of idling errors that occur when qubits remain inactive during waiting periods within a quantum circuit. Conventional mitigation techniques, such as dynamical decoupling, suppress decoherence by periodically refreshing quantum states through the insertion of additional control gates. In this paper, we propose an alternative approach that suppresses idling errors through quantum circuit scheduling without introducing any additional gate operations. By appropriately adjusting the execution timing of quantum gates with scheduling flexibility, we demonstrate through both numerical simulations and hardware experiments that the overall computational accuracy can be significantly influenced and, in many cases, improved. In addition, we analytically derive the density-matrix evolution under idling noise and provide a theoretical framework that explains the observed behavior.

similar_to.title: Dynamical decoupling for superconducting qubits: a performance survey
Erasure qubits: Overcoming the $T_1$ limit in superconducting circuits

summary.summary: This paper proposes suppressing idling errors in superconducting qubits through circuit scheduling that adjusts the timing of Hadamard gates within idle intervals, without inserting additional control pulses. Two strategies are introduced—midpoint placement and random shot-by-shot placement—and validated on a 64-qubit superconducting processor with measured coherence times $T_1 = 5.24$–$32.81$ μs and $T_2 = 8.44$–$43.34$ μs, showing improvements up to 12% in accuracy compared to unfavorable placements.
summary.motivation: Idling errors from amplitude damping, dephasing, and frequency drift accumulate when qubits remain inactive during circuit execution, particularly in circuits requiring SWAP gates for quantum error correction. Dynamical decoupling mitigates this but introduces gate-fidelity errors; a control-free alternative is needed.
summary.method: Two heuristic scheduling rules are proposed: placing H gates at the temporal midpoint of idle intervals, or sampling insertion times uniformly over each shot and averaging outcomes. The density-matrix evolution under combined amplitude damping ($\gamma = 1 - e^{-t/T_1}$), dephasing ($\lambda = 1 - e^{-t/T_2}/2$), and quasi-static detuning ($\delta\omega$) is analytically derived; trace distance is used to quantify fidelity loss. Hardware experiments on single- and two-qubit circuits, plus QuTiP simulations with Haar-random initial states, validate the approach.
summary.result: Midpoint placement and random placement both yield near-optimal performance in the practically relevant regime ($T \lesssim 6$ μs for two-qubit states), avoiding worst-case exposure to either amplitude damping or dephasing. For unknown initial states, both strategies reduce Haar-averaged trace distance by up to 12% at $T = 5$ μs; analytical results confirm that the midpoint achieves the global minimum when accumulated phase $\omega T \leq \pi/2$ and remains robust beyond this via symmetry-breaking effects that typically shift the optimum by $< 1\%$.
